<p className="eyebrow">The tools</p>

# Environments

<div className="lede">
Two questions with one answer here: which Node, Bun or pnpm each command runs
on — declared in `uf.config.js` where it is used, locked in `uf.lock`, installed
into a store shared by every repository on the machine — and where the values
in `process.env` and `import.meta.env` come from, which is the `.env` cascade at
the bottom of this page.
</div>

**What you will be able to do:** declare the runtime and package manager each
command runs on, lock them so every machine runs the same releases, see which
release a command will use and which key chose it, install them ahead of time,
move a project off `env.toolchain`, and decide where the values in
`process.env` come from.

**What you need first:** a project — [Your first project](/guide/project). A
release you declare with a version is installed for you, so the machine does
not need to have it already.

## Declaring the tools

<div className="command"><code>uf.config.js</code></div>

```js
// @flow
import { defineConfig } from "@uniflowed/config";

export default defineConfig({
  runtime: "node@24",
  packageManager: "pnpm@10",
  build: { runtime: "node@26" },
  test: { runtime: "bun@1.4" },
});
```

Each key names a tool where it is used, which is also what the tool is for.
This project serves on Node 24, builds on Node 26, runs its tests on Bun 1.4
and installs with pnpm 10, and every machine that checks it out runs those
four.

| Command | Runs on |
| --- | --- |
| `uf dev`, `uf build`, `uf preview` | `build.runtime`, then `runtime` |
| `uf test` | `test.runtime`, then the runtime `test.runner` brings, then `runtime` |
| `uf start`, `uf run`, `uf exec` | `runtime` |
| `uf install`, `uf add`, `uf remove`, `uf update` and the other package commands | `packageManager`, then `pm.packageManager`, then `package.json#packageManager`, then the lockfiles |

The first key in a row that says something decides. A project that writes none
of them runs as it did before they existed: on the host
[`app.runtime.capabilityJsHost`](/reference/config#app) finds, with the manager
[Dependencies](/guide/dependencies#which-manager-runs) describes.

`runtime`, `build.runtime` and `test.runtime` name `node`, `bun` or `deno`, and
`packageManager` names `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn` or `bun`. Two more keys sit beside
them. `build.builder` is the builder `uf dev` and `uf build` drive: `"vite"`,
which is `@uniflowed/vite` and the default, or a module of your own.
`test.runner` is `"uf"`, the runner built into uf and the default; `"bun@1.4"`
is read, and `uf test` refuses it until `bun test` can run behind `uf test`
([#942](https://github.com/ubugeeei-prod/uf/issues/942)).

### Writing a version

A tool is written `name[@version]`:

| Written | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `"node"` | whichever `node` is on `PATH` — a machine without one is refused, not handed another runtime |
| `"node@26"` | the newest 26.x, resolved the first time a command needs it and locked in `uf.lock` |
| `"node@26.8.2"` | exactly that release |
| `"node@^26"`, `"node@>=24"` | refused |

A prefix is the one to reach for. It keeps the repository on a line of
releases without anyone having to choose a patch, and the lock makes every
machine agree on the patch anyway. A range is refused, because a range is not
an environment: it answers "what could this build with", and the question a
repository has to answer is what it *is* built with.

```
error: /app/uf.config.js: build.runtime is `node@^26`, which is a range, and a range is not an environment: it can resolve to a different release tomorrow. Write a version prefix instead — `node@26` is the newest 26.x, resolved once and locked in uf.lock
```

## The first run

<div className="command"><code>uf build</code></div>

```
› build.runtime is `node@26`: locked at 26.8.2 in uf.lock
› installing node@26.8.2 for build.runtime — once, into the store every project on this machine shares
```

The first command that needs `node@26` reads the publisher's release list —
nodejs.org's for Node, the npm registry's for Bun, Deno, npm, pnpm and Yarn —
and writes the newest match into `uf.lock`:

<div className="command"><code>uf.lock</code></div>

```json
{
  "toolchain": {
    "node@26": "26.8.2"
  }
}
```

Commit it. From then on the lock is the answer on every machine, CI included,
and no release list is read to decide it again; moving to a newer 26.x is
`uf env update`, below. A `uf.lock` that holds only this record says nothing
about which package manager installs the project.

The release is installed the first time a command needs it, and each of those
firsts is said once, as above. Offline, or on a platform the publisher ships no
build for, the command stops and names the key and the spec rather than running
on whatever `node` is on `PATH`:

```
error: test.runtime is `node@99.0.1`, and node@99.0.1 could not be installed
```

Starting the pinned binary is half of running on it. Vite's workers, a plugin
that shells out, a test that spawns `node` and every `#!/usr/bin/env node` bin
in `node_modules/.bin` find their runtime on `PATH`, so the runtime's directory
goes first on `PATH` for everything the command starts: a `node` that
`uf build` starts above is 26.8.2 as well.

The package manager is the same. With `packageManager: "pnpm@10"`, `uf install`
runs the pnpm `uf.lock` locks, from the store, and the `node` that pnpm starts
on is `runtime`'s. `uf install --frozen-lockfile`, the install CI runs, changes
no lockfile, so a prefix `uf.lock` does not lock yet is refused there rather
than resolved: run `uf install` once and commit `uf.lock`.

## Seeing what runs

<div className="command"><code>uf explain build</code></div>

```
    3. JavaScript host
        provider  node 26.8.2
        what      runs the builder and any JavaScript plugin; `build.runtime` names node@26, locked at 26.8.2 in uf.lock; in the store, and first on PATH for every process it starts
```

`uf explain <command>` names the release the command runs on, the key that
chose it, the lock, and whether the store has it yet. It reads rather than
resolves, so explaining a command never downloads what it explains. `uf inspect`
lists every tool at once:

<div className="command"><code>uf inspect</code></div>

```
  tools
    runtime          node@24 (runtime) · locked at 24.21.0
    build runtime    node@26 (build.runtime) · locked at 26.8.2
    test runtime     bun@1.4 (test.runtime) · locked at 1.4.2
    test runner      uf (uf's default)
    package manager  pnpm@10 (packageManager) · locked at 10.34.5
    builder          vite (uf's default)
```

## Installing ahead of time

<div className="command"><code>uf env install</code></div>

```
uf env install · my-app
───────────────────────

  - node@24 (24.21.0)  runtime  installed
  - node@26 (26.8.2)  build runtime  installed
  - bun@1.4 (1.4.2)  test runtime  installed
  - pnpm@10 (10.34.5)  package manager  installed

› locked node@24 at 24.21.0, node@26 at 26.8.2, bun@1.4 at 1.4.2, pnpm@10 at 10.34.5 in uf.lock
✓ 6 executables linked into ~/.local/share/uf/envs/my-app-4f2a1c8e93b0d571/bin
```

Everything a command would install the first time it needs it, installed now —
what a CI image, or a laptop about to go offline, wants. `uf env install`
installs every tool the project declares at a version: `runtime`,
`build.runtime`, `test.runtime`, `packageManager`, the older `env.toolchain`,
and an exact version in `package.json#engines`. A prefix nothing has locked yet
is resolved and locked on the way.

Each tool is unpacked once, into a store keyed by tool, version and platform —
`node-26.8.2-darwin-arm64` — and every repository that wants that exact release
uses the same copy. Two projects on the same Node share it; a third on a
different one gets its own, and neither disturbs the other.

uf writes in four places and no others: the store, the per-project link
directory beside it, the `toolchain` record in `uf.lock`, and `.uf/profile` in
the repository once you have picked an environment. There is no `sudo` step, no
shell profile to edit, and no version manager to initialise in your `.zshrc`.
The download's checksum is verified before anything is unpacked, against the
digest the publisher ships beside the archive.

The store lives under `$XDG_DATA_HOME/uf/store`, and `$UF_STORE` overrides
it; the links live beside it under `uf/envs`, and `$UF_ENVS` overrides those.

<div className="command"><code>uf env list</code></div>

```
uf env · my-app
───────────────

  this project
    - node@24 (24.21.0)  runtime  installed
    - node@26 (26.8.2)  build runtime  installed
    - bun@1.4 (1.4.2)  test runtime  installed
    - pnpm@10 (10.34.5)  package manager  installed

  the store
    at  ~/.local/share/uf/store
    - bun-1.4.2-darwin-arm64
    - node-24.21.0-darwin-arm64
    - node-26.8.2-darwin-arm64
    - pnpm-10.34.5-darwin-arm64
```

shows each tool, what it is for and whether the store has it, beside what the
store holds for every repository. It reads `uf.lock` and fetches nothing, so a
prefix nothing has locked yet is shown as not locked.

<div className="command"><code>uf env update</code></div>

reads each publisher's release list again and moves every prefix in `uf.lock` to
its newest release, printing what moved — `node@26  26.8.2 → 26.9.0`. It
installs nothing: the change is a line in `uf.lock` to review, and the next
command that needs the new release installs it.

## Using the tools outside a command

<div className="command"><code>uf env exec node --version</code></div>

```
v24.21.0
```

`uf env exec` puts the project's tools in front of `PATH` for one command and
runs it, exiting with whatever the command exited with. The `node` there is
`runtime`'s, the one the application itself runs on. The shell you are in is
unchanged, and so is every other repository on the machine.

The links are beside the store rather than inside the project, in a directory
named for the project and keyed by its path — which keeps the property that
made them per-project in the first place: two checkouts on different Node
versions sit beside each other and neither is "active". What it drops is a
directory nobody wrote, nobody reads and every `.gitignore` had to know about.
`$UF_ENVS` moves them.

That is the whole model, and it is `nix develop`'s: an environment is something
a directory *has*, not something a shell is switched into. Nothing has to be
activated, nothing has to be deactivated, and a script that runs `uf env exec`
gets the same tools whether it was started from your shell, from an editor, or
from CI.

## Collecting what nothing uses

<div className="command"><code>uf env gc</code></div>

```
  repositories that are gone
    - /Users/you/src/old-project (gone)

  removed
    - node-24.14.0-darwin-arm64
    - pnpm-9.15.0-darwin-arm64

✓ removed 2 entries, forgot 1 root; 0 entries in use
```

A store that only grows is a store nobody trusts. Every `uf env install`
registers the repository as a *root*, and so does a command that installs a
tool the first time it needs it. The collector keeps exactly what some live
root reaches: a repository that was deleted stops holding its tools, in the
same pass that notices it is gone.

<div className="command"><code>uf env gc --dry-run</code></div>

says what would go and removes nothing, which is the version to run first.

## Moving from env.toolchain

Before these keys, a repository pinned its tools in one list:

```js
export default defineConfig({
  env: { toolchain: { node: "24.14.0", pnpm: "9.15.0" } },
});
```

That list says *which* tools a repository has and nothing about what each one
is for, so no command ran on them; only `uf env exec` used them. It still works
— `uf env install` installs it — and every command that reads the config says
what to write instead:

```
! env.toolchain says which tools this project has and not what each is for; declare each where it is used instead — `runtime: "node@24.14.0"` and `packageManager: "pnpm@9.15.0"`
```

The other keys these replace work the same way: each keeps working, and each
says what replaces it.

| Was | Is |
| --- | --- |
| `env: { toolchain: { … } }` | `runtime`, `build.runtime`, `test.runtime` and `packageManager`, each where it is used |
| `pm: { packageManager: "pnpm" }` | `packageManager: "pnpm"`, which can pin a release as well |
| `builder: { module: "@uniflowed/vite" }` | `build: { builder: "vite" }` |
| `test: { runner: { … } }` | `test: { runner: "uf" }`, or nothing, since it is the default |

A `test.runner` object that sets `applicationTarget` to something other than
what `app.framework` implies has no other spelling yet. Keep it until
[#953](https://github.com/ubugeeei-prod/uf/issues/953) gives it one; uf says so
rather than telling you to delete it.

An old key and its replacement can sit side by side while they say the same
thing. When they disagree, the config is refused naming both, because which one
you meant is not a question uf gets to answer by precedence:

```
error: /app/uf.config.js: runtime is `node@26` and env.toolchain.node is `24.14.0` — two spellings of one tool that disagree, and uf does not pick one. env.toolchain.node is the deprecated spelling: delete `env.toolchain.node`, and write `runtime: "node@24.14.0"` if 24.14.0 is the release you mean.
```

## What the toolchain half does not do

It does not manage the uf binary itself — that is `uf use` and `uf self-update`.
It does not read `.nvmrc` or `.tool-versions`: `uf.config.js` is the one place a
uf project writes down what it runs on, and a second source of truth for the
same question is the problem, not the feature. `package.json#engines` is read
for one thing, which is that `uf env install` installs an exact version written
there. No command runs on it, because a range there is a statement about
compatibility rather than a choice of release. And `uf build --compile` still
embeds the host `app.runtime.capabilityJsHost` finds rather than `runtime`
([#1036](https://github.com/ubugeeei-prod/uf/issues/1036)).

## Environment variables

Everything above is about tools. This is about values: a URL, a feature flag, a
database password — the things that differ between your laptop, CI and
production, and that must not be committed as code.

<div className="command"><code>.env</code></div>

```
# Anything the browser may see starts with VITE_.
VITE_API_URL=https://api.example.com

# Anything else is the server's alone.
DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost/app
```

<div className="command"><code>app/$page.js</code></div>

```js
// @flow
import * as React from "@uniflowed/react";

export component Page() {
  // Substituted at build time, and it is in the bundle the browser downloads.
  return <a href={String(import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL)}>the API</a>;
}
```

Server code — a route handler, a loader, a component that only ever renders on
the server — reads every variable through `process.env` instead, including the
ones with no prefix.

`uf dev`, `uf build`, `uf preview`, `uf start`, `uf test`, `uf run` and `uf exec`
all read the same files the same way. A value that reaches the dev server and
not the build is a bug, not a setting.

### Which files, and in what order

A command runs in a **mode**, and the mode picks two of the four files:

| File | When it is read | Commit it? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.env` | always | yes |
| `.env.local` | always | no — this is your machine's |
| `.env.<mode>` | in that mode | yes |
| `.env.<mode>.local` | in that mode | no |

They are read **in that order, and the last one to set a name wins**. So
`.env.production` beats `.env`, and `.env.production.local` beats both. A file
that is not there is skipped, which is why `.env.local` can be in
`.gitignore` and nothing breaks on a machine that has never had one.

`uf new` writes `.env.local` and `.env.*.local` into `.gitignore`, because
those two are where a credential goes; the tracked `.env` and `.env.<mode>` are
the project's defaults and belong in the repository. Vite's dev server refuses
to serve any of them over HTTP whatever else is configured — see
[`docs/security.md`](https://github.com/ubugeeei-prod/uf/blob/main/docs/security.md).

### The mode

`development` for `uf dev`, `production` for `uf build`, `uf preview` and `uf
start`, `test` for `uf test`, `development` for `uf run` and `uf exec`. It is
also what the browser reads as `import.meta.env.MODE`.

Four ways to say otherwise, and they are tried in this order:

1. `--mode <name>` on the command: `uf build --mode staging` reads
   `.env.staging` and builds with `import.meta.env.MODE === "staging"`.
2. The profile `uf env use <name>` recorded, in `.uf/profile`. It is a local
   choice — a scaffolded project already ignores `.uf/` — and it lasts until
   you change it.
3. `env.active` in `uf.config.js`, for a project whose default mode is not one
   of the usual ones.
4. The command's own default, above.

A mode becomes the end of a file name, so it may hold letters, digits, `_`, `-`
and `.` and nothing else. `local` is refused, because `.env.local` is already
the file that overrides every mode.

The mode chooses files; it does not choose optimisations. `uf build --mode
staging` is still a production build — minified, with `import.meta.env.PROD`
true — because that is what building means. The one variable that changes it is
`NODE_ENV`, which is an ordinary variable here and which Vite reads: a file that
sets `NODE_ENV=development` makes even `uf build` produce a development build.
If you did not mean that, do not put `NODE_ENV` in a `.env` file.

<div className="command"><code>uf env use staging</code></div>

```
✓ mode staging: `.env`, `.env.local`, `.env.staging` and `.env.staging.local`, in .uf/profile
```

### The environment always wins

A variable that is already set when uf starts is never overwritten by a file:

<div className="command"><code>DATABASE_URL=postgres://prod/app uf build</code></div>

uses that one, whatever `.env.production` says. That is what makes a `.env` file
a default rather than a policy, and it is why a CI secret, a container's
environment and a `docker run -e` all keep working with no configuration at all.

`uf inspect` prints the mode, the files that were read and how many variables
came out of them — names only, never values, because that output ends up in
issues.

### What reaches the browser

**Only a name that starts with the client prefix — `VITE_`, until a project
sets another.** That value is substituted into the JavaScript the browser
downloads, so it is public: anyone who opens the site can
read it. Everything else is available to server code through `process.env` and
is never written into a client bundle, even if a module that ships to the
browser asks for it — `import.meta.env.DATABASE_URL` in client code is
`undefined`, not the password.

That boundary is Vite's, uf does not widen it, and there is a test that a value
without the prefix is absent from every file in `dist/`
(`crates/uf_cli/tests/vite.rs`). A project that prefers another prefix sets
Vite's own option, `vite: { envPrefix: "PUBLIC_" }`, and uf honours it. An empty
prefix is refused — by Vite, which throws on it, and by uf, which goes on using
`VITE_` — because it would put every variable in the bundle.

The rule to hold on to: **if it is a secret, it must not start with the
prefix.**

### The file format

One `NAME=value` a line, and:

```
# A comment. Blank lines are ignored.
export ALSO_FINE=yes          # `export ` is allowed, and ignored

QUOTED="  spaces are kept  "  # a trailing comment needs a space in front
LITERAL='no $expansion, no \n escapes, exactly as written'
MULTILINE="first line
second line"

ESCAPES="a tab\there and a newline\nthere"
HASH=pass#word                # no space in front, so it is part of the value

HOST=example.com
API_URL=https://${HOST}/api   # or $HOST, without the braces
PRICE=costs \$5               # a literal dollar
```

* A name starts with a letter or `_` and continues with letters, digits or `_`.
* Double quotes understand `\n`, `\r`, `\t`, `\\`, `\"`, `\'` and `\$`; a
  backslash before anything else is a backslash, so a Windows path survives.
* Single quotes are exactly as written: no escapes, no expansion.
* Both may span lines.
* `$NAME` and `${NAME}` expand to something **already defined** — earlier in
  this file, in a file earlier in the cascade, or in the environment. The
  environment's value is the one that expands, since that is the value the name
  will have.

A file that does not parse **stops the command**, and the message names the file,
the line and what to do:

```
error: failed to load the environment files for mode development
  caused by: /app/.env:2: `${HSOT}` is not defined; define it earlier, set it in
  the environment, or write `\${HSOT}` for a literal dollar
```

An undefined expansion is an error rather than an empty string, and that is a
decision: `https://$HSOT/api` silently becoming `https:///api` is a typo that
reaches production and fails somewhere else entirely.

### Naming the files yourself

<div className="command"><code>uf.config.js</code></div>

```js
// @flow
export default {
  env: {
    files: ["config/shared.env", "config/local.env"],
  },
};
```

Replaces the cascade entirely: those files, in that order, later winning,
relative to the project root, and no `.env` anything. Empty by default, which is
what selects the four files above.

Inside the project, and only inside it. An absolute path, a `..`, a `~` and a
symlink that points out are all refused, whichever of the files it is: a
`uf.config.js` in a repository you have just cloned is not a thing that should
be able to read `~/.aws/credentials` — which parses as `NAME=value` like
anything else — into the environment of every command you then run. See
[`docs/security.md`](https://github.com/ubugeeei-prod/uf/blob/main/docs/security.md).

### What the variables half does not do

* **It does not reload in place.** `uf dev` does watch the files the cascade
  selects, and starts the server again when one of them changes, saying which
  file it was — so an edit no longer needs you to restart the command by hand.
  What it will not do is swap the value into a running page. A restart is the
  honest granularity: a prefixed value reaches the browser by being substituted
  into the bundle, so a new one has to be substituted again and every module
  that read it has to be evaluated again. `uf build`, `uf preview` and
  `uf start` read the files once, which is all a command that ends has to do.
* **It does not travel to a deployment.** `uf build --adapter node` writes a
  directory that a host runs with plain `node server.js`, and that process is
  not uf: it reads its environment from the host, which is where a deployment's
  secrets belong anyway. The values a *build* needed are already in the bundle;
  the ones the server needs are the host's to provide.
* **It is not a secret store.** A `.env` file is a file on a disk. uf refuses to
  serve one over HTTP and refuses to put an unprefixed one in a bundle, and
  neither of those makes it encrypted.
